issueThreads.author: RobaireTH
issueThreads.body: ## Project Summary pckt is a red-packet style application built on CKB. A sender seals an amount of CKB into a single live packet cell governed by a custom Rust lock script, then shares a claim link. Recipients open the link and each claim consumes the packet cell and produces its next version, so the chain itself is the source of truth for who has claimed and how much is left. If all slots are claimed the packet terminates; if it expires first, the sender can reclaim the remainder. Three modes are supported: **fixed** (every recipient gets the same amount), **lucky split** (random non-last payouts with a contract-enforced 63 CKB minimum so no slot goes below cell-rent), and **timed unlock** (sealed until a wall-clock time, then everyone can claim). ## Tools used - **Contract**: Rust + `ckb-std` 0.18, `molecule`, `blake2b-ref`, `k256` (compiled to `riscv64imac-unknown-none-elf`) - **Frontend**: React 18 + TypeScript + Vite, `@ckb-ccc/connector-react` for wallet connect and transaction building, `@noble/secp256k1` for claim-secret signing - **Backend**: Rust + Axum + SQLite indexer, deployed on Fly.io (single shared-CPU machine + persistent volume) - **Hosting**: Vercel (frontend), Fly.io (backend), CKB testnet (Pudge) RPC + indexer - **CLI / deploy**: `ckb-cli` for keystore-signed contract deploys ## Current features - Seal a packet on-chain in fixed, lucky-split, or timed-unlock mode (2–50 slots) - Claim by link — the claim secret lives in the URL fragment so it never touches the backend - Lucky split with on-chain enforced 63 CKB per-slot minimum (just redeployed on testnet) - Timed-unlock packets that reject claims before the unlock timestamp - Reclaim flow for expired packets, wired into the sender UI - Sender-side dashboard: active packets, claimed activity, expired and reclaimable - Sender profile labels (backend-stored, convenience naming) - In-app notifications feed for claim and reclaim events - Short links (`pckt-backend.fly.dev/s/`) generated from an OS CSPRNG with an allow-listed target host set - Reorg-aware indexer that rolls back state by block hash on chain reorganizations - Per-IP rate limiting with a bounded bucket map and an opt-in trusted-proxy mode ## Planned features - **Decentralized sender identity**: replace backend-stored profile labels with on-chain or signed-attestation identity so naming is portable and self-sovereign - **Multi-code-hash indexer**: track multiple historical contract code hashes so packet redeploys don't strand in-flight packets in the UI - **Lower cell-rent floor**: redesign the packet's data layout (likely a Merkle commitment for `claimed_locks` instead of an inline array) to reduce the minimum capacity each packet needs to occupy - **Mainnet readiness pass**: dust-attack analysis, fee-rate adaptation, signed-relay auditing - **Better recipient UX for heavy locks**: contract-side or frontend-side adaptation of the per-slot minimum based on the recipient's actual lock script (multisig / type-script-bearing wallets need more than 63 CKB) - **Group / event mode**: time-bounded events where multiple senders fund a shared pool and recipients claim once across the whole event ## Deployed on - **Testnet (Pudge)** — current active deployment. - Active code hash: `0x5d70f3f6754486b9d666868455376931f2d6babb3593256a1fa2ab3218d7cbc1` - Deploy tx: `0x188f0773ab503f69cfd0dc23fb4a89e5fe321274348ce5db9f8fd5bb74206e83` - `hash_type`: `data1` ## Link to repository https://github.com/RobaireTH/pckt ## Link to hosted version of project https://sendpckt.robaireth.dev ## Screenshots ## Request for feedback ### Problems 1. **The cell-rent floor is non-trivial.** A packet's minimum capacity is dominated by the inline `claimed_locks` array, which scales with slot count. For 50-slot lucky packets that's a meaningful fraction of the total. I have a rough plan to swap to a Merkle commitment but want a sanity check before doing the rewrite. 2. **Lucky split's last-slot windfall is structural, not stylistic.** The final claimer drains the cell, which means they receive the cell-rent floor on top of the random remainder. This is a property of CKB's cell model rather than something the lock script chose, but it does surprise users. I'd like input on whether masking it (e.g. capping the last slot to the same distribution as earlier slots and burning the dust) is worth the cost. ### Review I'm asking reviewers to assess: - **Contract design**: is the single-cell model the right choice for this use case? Particular interest in claim-path edge cases (script reuse across claims, cell-dep stability across redeploys, witness-layout choices). - **Backend non-authority boundary**: is the line between "UX helper" and "trust anchor" actually clean in the current code, or are there places where the frontend silently relies on the backend in a way that would break if it were swapped out? - **Concept viability**: does the red-packet UX translate cleanly to CKB's strengths, and does the implementation make those strengths visible to a user, or is the cell model an implementation detail nobody can see? ### Guidance I'd appreciate concrete advice on: - The right path from testnet to a credible mainnet deployment . What hardening would *you* want to see before signing a real-funds packet? - Whether the planned data-layout redesign (Merkle commitment for claimed locks) is worth the contract complexity given the current floor, or whether there's a simpler shape I'm missing. - Whether decentralized sender identity should be a wallet-level concern (e.g. a signed-attestation pattern the wallet provides) or whether pckt should ship its own primitive and if so, what minimum primitive would be useful to other CKB apps too (DID). - Distribution: where does a CKB-native app actually find users today, and what's the bar to graduate from "demo on testnet" to "people send each other pckts because they want to"?

# Review of `pckt` — Code-level Findings + Answers to Feedback Questions

I went through the contract (`main.rs`, `schema.mol`, `integration.rs`), the backend (routes / indexer / rate_limit / db), the frontend (`tx.ts`, `Claim.tsx`, `packets.ts`, `molecule.ts`), and the Dockerfile / deployment metadata. Below is a layered set of findings, followed by direct answers to the four feedback questions in the issue.

---

## 1) Contract

The overall design is solid. A single-cell state machine, `claim`/`reclaim` union witness, signature bound to `outpoint || claimer_lock_hash`, and strict field-equality checks on the successor — these are the right "chain-as-truth" choices.

### What's done correctly

- `RecipientHasData` (commit `a1124c0`) rejecting recipient cells that carry data is a good fix; otherwise a malicious claimer could attach a type-script and turn a payout cell into a token-bearing dust.
- `find_unique_successor_output_index` in `main.rs:197-214` matches the successor by group-input lock hash and forces uniqueness — this kills any split/merge attack on the packet cell.
- Signature verification in `main.rs:354-373` uses `recover_from_prehash` and compares the recovered 33-byte compressed pubkey rather than a hashed equality check; that is the correct ECDSA recovery pattern.
- The signed message is `blake2b(out_point || claimer_lock_hash)`. Binding outpoint into the message is what prevents replaying a claim signature against a different successor cell. Important.

### Suggestions / risks

1. **`max_floor` reserves capacity for `slots_total - 1` lock hashes up front** (`main.rs:219`). This is what makes the cell-rent floor large, but it's also what guarantees that the final successor never hits `InsufficientCellCapacity` because every prior claimer "pre-paid" the storage for the not-yet-claimed slots' hashes. Correct, but it's the root cause of the floor problem (see Q1 in the feedback section).

2. **`compute_payout` in lucky mode uses `seed % range` where `seed = blake2b(salt || slot_idx)`** (`main.rs:251-257`). Since `salt` lives in the cell data and is public, **anyone with the link can compute exactly how much each future slot will pay before they claim**. This is currently used by `predictClaimPayout` in the frontend (`packets.ts:137`) to render a preview, but if "you don't know how much until you open" is part of the product surprise, it isn't actually surprising — it's a UX illusion. If you want true commit-reveal randomness, mix the previous tx's outpoint into the seed (you already use the outpoint in the signature path); the next slot's payout would then be unknowable until the previous claim is mined.

3. **`enforce_invariants` allows `slots_total = 1`** (`main.rs:404-406`). A 1-slot lucky packet falls through into the `remaining_slots == 1` branch and just drains the cell — semantically equivalent to a transfer. Not a bug, but inconsistent with the "2–50 slots" wording in the issue. The frontend already gates this in `CreateAmount.tsx`; nothing to do on-chain.

4. **`enforce_no_double_claim` is `O(N)` linear scan** (`main.rs:319-328`). Fine at N=50, but it becomes the obvious cycle-bottleneck if you migrate to a Merkle commitment — you'd replace it with an SMT non-membership proof, which has very different cycle characteristics.

5. **`enforce_claim_timing` strictly requires `since == 0` for non-timed packets** (`main.rs:336-338`). Good "whitelist" style — prevents anyone from smuggling commit-reveal data through `since` later.

6. **Witness layout is action-only** (`PacketWitness { action: union(Claim, Reclaim) }`). Clean. Lots of CKB lock scripts overload the witness with `since` / `header_idx` / version bytes; you didn't, and it shrinks the attack surface meaningfully.

---

## 2) Backend — the "trust anchor" boundary

This is the most important section because one of your feedback questions is exactly about it. There are concrete leaks today.

### 2.1 Critical: `/v1/profiles` accepts arbitrary writes for any `owner_lock_hash`

`profiles.rs:75-109` upserts `(owner_lock_hash, sender_address, username)` with **no proof that the requester actually controls the lock_hash**. Schema `20260430010000_sender_profiles.sql` keys on `owner_lock_hash`; last writer wins. The profile is then JOINed into `/v1/packets` (`packets.rs:52-61`), so every list-packets response can echo a forged `owner_address` / `owner_name`.

The frontend partially mitigates this: `ownerLabel` in `packets.ts:95-115` only shows `ownerName` if the viewer is the owner. So the username field is "fool yourself only." But `ownerAddress` is shown to everyone, and an attacker can register an arbitrary string against someone else's lock hash, so the displayed sender address is forgeable.

**Fixes, cheapest to most thorough:**

- **Free fix**: validate `script_hash(parse(sender_address)) == owner_lock_hash` server-side. The relationship is publicly derivable, so this isn't an authentication step — it's just declining nonsensical inputs. Stops 100% of "register lock-hash A with address B" abuse.
- **Light auth**: challenge–response. Server issues a nonce, client wallet signs `nonce || owner_lock_hash || username`, server verifies. This is the minimum implementation of the "signed-attestation pattern" you mention in the planned features.
- **Fully decentralized**: don't ship your own primitive — integrate an existing CKB DID (see Q3 in feedback below).

### 2.2 Medium: reorg rollback can delete still-valid packet rows

`db/blocks.rs:46-50`:

```sql
DELETE FROM packets WHERE last_seen_block >= ?1
```

Scenario: packet sealed at block 100, claimed at block 150. The claim handler upserts the successor row and `mark_terminal`s the original — both rows now have `last_seen_block = 150`. If a reorg starts at block 145:

- block_hashes / packet_events at ≥145 are deleted ✓
- successor row deleted ✓
- **the original packet row is also deleted**, even though the seal tx is in block 100 and is still on the canonical chain ✗

Then the indexer resumes scanning from 145 forward, never re-sees the seal tx (it's at block 100), and the packet permanently disappears from the backend. `BACKFILL_THRESHOLD = 1024` and `REORG_DEPTH = 50` make this rare in practice, but the logic is still wrong for any reorg shorter than 50 blocks that crosses a claim.

**Suggested fix**: maintain an append-only `packet_states` history (`out_point, block_number, snapshot_blob`); on rollback, delete rows ≥`from` and rebuild `packets` from the max remaining block per outpoint. Or, less elegantly, trigger a full `backfill()` on every rollback.

### 2.3 Medium: `/v1/relay/tx` is an unrestricted CKB tx forwarder

`relay.rs:21-37` only checks that `signed_tx` is a JSON object before forwarding to `send_transaction`. The `Origin` header is enforced by browsers, but any non-browser client can spoof Origin to hit the allowlist. Combined with the 5 RPS rate limit, abuse is bounded but real — anyone can use this endpoint as a free CKB JSON-RPC relay for *any* tx.

**Cheap fix**: deserialize `signed_tx` and assert that at least one input cell's lock or one cell_dep matches `PCKT_LOCK.code_hash`. Turns this into a packet-only relay with one `serde_json::from_value` call.

### 2.4 Minor (currently dead code, but a footgun): `/v1/messages` doesn't validate `hash == blake160(body)`

`messages.rs:36-64` accepts `(message_hash, body)` and stores them verbatim. The frontend doesn't currently call this endpoint, but if you wire it up later for long messages, you must validate `blake160(body) == message_hash` before insert; otherwise an attacker can squat any hash with bogus content. `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` makes the squat permanent.

### 2.5 Minor: rate-limit reads the leftmost `X-Forwarded-For` entry

`rate_limit.rs:96-102` takes XFF[0] when `trust_forwarded_for=true`. That's correct behind a single trusted edge proxy, but any client can set `X-Forwarded-For: <spoofed>, <real-ip>` and inject a fresh per-IP bucket on every request. On Fly.io specifically, prefer `Fly-Client-IP`, or count from the right by the number of trusted hops. Deployment-level concern, not a code bug.

### 2.6 Minor: indexer is hard-coded to a single `code_hash`

`runner.rs:122-145` and `collect_new_packets` filter by `state.config.packet_lock.code_hash` as a single value. This is exactly the "multi-code-hash indexer" you list as a planned feature. Practical effect today: every redeploy strands all in-flight packets in the UI. Cheapest implementation: change `packet_lock` to `Vec<PacketLock>` with `since_block` and switch the filter from equality to `set.contains`.

### 2.7 Smaller observations

- `links.rs:122-126` — the slug generator uses `b % 32` over a 32-byte alphabet. 256 / 32 is exact, so no modulo bias. Correct.
- The shortlink target host allowlist + sweeper (`lib.rs:76-90`) is the right defense against open-redirect abuse. Good.
- `routes/relay.rs:39-63` translates on-chain error codes (e.g. `error code 55`) to user-readable messages by *string-matching* the RPC error envelope. Will silently degrade to the generic message if ckb-rpc tweaks its formatting. Already covered by unit tests, which is the right way to keep this honest.
- SQLite under concurrent writes (indexer + user POSTs) needs WAL. Make sure the sqlx connection string has `?journal_mode=WAL&busy_timeout=...`.
- `Dockerfile` pins `rust:1.93-slim-bookworm`. That image doesn't exist as of writing — likely a typo for 1.83. Also, `cargo build` without `--locked` can pull a different `Cargo.lock` resolution under CI than locally.

---

## 3) Frontend

- **The claim secret never touches the backend.** `Claim.tsx:31-41` parses `sk` from the URL fragment, and `tx.ts:149` only sends the *pubkey hash* to the server when generating the share link. This matches the architecture described in the issue.
- **Fee estimation order in `buildAndRelayClaimTx`** (`tx.ts:221-228`) is `completeFeeBy → setWitnessArgsAt(0) → signTransaction`. The fee is therefore computed against a tx that doesn't yet contain the ~110-byte claim witness, so the actual on-chain tx is slightly larger than the size used for fee estimation. Reclaim path (`tx.ts:260-261`) does it in the correct order; please swap the two lines in claim too.
- **`predictClaimPayout`** in `packets.ts:137-159` re-implements the contract's lucky-split formula and matches it bit-for-bit (`(seed % range) + lower` on chain vs `lower + (seed % range)` on the client). Verified consistent.
- **`predictClaimPayout` doesn't account for the recipient's actual cell-rent minimum.** `Claim.tsx:75-84` does surface the `claimCapacityError` *at claim time*, which is good. But your "Better recipient UX for heavy locks" planned item should be done at **seal time**: the current `SAFE_SLOT_PAYOUT_SHANNONS = 70 CKB` is a static constant; for users with multisig / type-script-bearing locks, that floor needs to scale with the recipient's lock script size before seal, otherwise lucky-split slots at the lower end of the range become unclaimable.
- **`headerDeps: [tipHash]`** in the claim tx (`tx.ts:197`) is unused by the lock script. CKB's absolute-timestamp `since` is enforced at consensus level (37-block median), no header dep needed and the script doesn't read one. Harmless redundancy.

---

## 4) Answers to the Feedback Questions

### Problems

**Q1: Is the cell-rent floor worth fixing via Merkle commitment for `claimed_locks`?**

**Yes — do the rewrite.**

- Current floor for 50-slot, empty-message packets: `(57 + 52 + 169 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 32×49) × 1e8 ≈ 185.4 CKB` of cell capacity locked just to hold the claimed-locks array. Replacing the array with a 32-byte SMT root drops that to ~30 CKB — a **~155 CKB reduction per packet**. That's the difference between "a 5 CKB lucky packet is feasible" and "everyone needs to seal at least 200 CKB."
- The complexity is bounded: replace `enforce_no_double_claim` with an SMT non-membership proof in the witness, and replace the `claimed_locks.len() == prev_len + 1` + tail-equality check in `verify_successor` with a `new_root == update(old_root, claimer_lock_hash)` check.
- Use SMT (key=lock_hash, value=1), not an in-witness Merkle list — sparse paths keep the witness much smaller than the current `Byte32Vec`.
- Trade-offs to be honest about: more cycles, more contract code, and clients now need to maintain a reproducible state to construct proofs (which they already do — they need the full `claimed_locks` array today anyway). Net: the floor reduction is product-defining.

**Q2: Mask the lucky-split last-slot windfall?**

**No, don't mask it.**

- The structural windfall (last claimer drains the cell and inherits the cell-rent floor) is a side effect of the cell model, but in red-packet culture an outsized last payout maps cleanly to the "压轴" (climax) idiom — it can be marketed as a feature rather than papered over.
- Masking would require either burning the dust (wasteful, ugly on-chain), or refunding to sender (drags sender into the claim tx, breaks the recipient-only-claim invariant). Neither is worth it.
- The right move is a one-line UI hint at claim time: *"the final claimer also receives the cell-rent deposit (~N CKB)."* Zero code change in the contract; reframe rather than redesign.

### Review

**Q: Is the single-cell model the right choice?**

Yes.

- Red-packet semantics — "N slots remaining; opening one consumes one and produces the next state" — *is* a state machine, and CKB's cell-as-state is the most direct mapping. The alternative (a type-script with a counter, owner-signed unlock) would force a single signing authority and lose the "anyone with the link can claim" property.
- The seal → claim₁ → ... → claimₙ chain forms an outpoint chain that *is* the source of truth for who claimed what. The indexer is just a cache. That alignment is exactly what the cell model is supposed to express.
- **Script-reuse-across-claims** is well-handled: same lock (args = `claim_pubkey_hash`, unchanged across versions) means `lock.hash()` is stable across all successors, which is what lets the indexer match successors via salt (`runner.rs:259-263`).
- **Cell-dep stability across redeploys**: `hash_type=data1` is the right choice — old packets stay bound to the old code blob and can't be reinterpreted by a new deployment. The cost is exactly the multi-code-hash indexer requirement, which you've already identified as planned.
- **Witness-layout choice**: action-only union (no extra fields) is clean and minimizes attack surface.

**Q: Is the backend non-authority boundary clean?**

**Not entirely — see §2.1–2.4.**

What would happen if someone replaced the backend tomorrow:
- Funds are safe — chain-side state is fully sufficient to reconstruct everything. So there's no "funds at risk" coupling.
- However, **`/v1/profiles` is a real trust-anchor leak**, because the data it stores doesn't exist on-chain and can't be re-derived. The frontend currently displays unverified `owner_address` to non-owners, which is forgeable. This is the most concrete form of "the frontend silently relies on the backend."
- A smaller leak: `Claim.tsx:71` reads `packet.message_body` directly from the backend response. The frontend already pulls the live packet cell via `signer.client.getCellLive(op)` in `tx.ts:162`, so it could decode `message` from on-chain data instead. That single change reduces the backend to a pure index/notification cache for everything UX-critical.

**Q: Does the red-packet UX surface CKB's strengths?**

For end users, no — and that's both good and bad. Good: "send 100 CKB → recipient claims" doesn't require understanding cells, which is correct UX. Bad: nothing on the surface tells the user this is different from an EVM red packet.

If you want CKB's model to be visible without compromising the main flow, consider a "see how this works on CKB" panel after seal/claim that explains:
1. Claiming consumed the original cell.
2. A new version of the cell was produced.
3. The off-chain indexer is just an observer.

Those three points are the cell-vs-account difference distilled. They also let you naturally lead into the *one* thing pckt does that EVM red packets fundamentally can't: the reclaim flow (`main.rs:274-308`) is unilaterally enforced by consensus — no admin key, no upgradeable contract, no front-runnable refund. That's a real differentiator and worth saying out loud in product copy.

### Guidance

**Pre-mainnet hardening checklist (in priority order):**

1. **Fix §2.1** — enforce `script_hash(address) == owner_lock_hash` on profile upsert. Non-negotiable; without this the displayed sender identity is forgeable.
2. **Fix §2.2** — replace the `last_seen_block ≥ from` rollback with a per-outpoint state-history table. Mainnet finality is stricter, but short reorgs still happen during congestion.
3. **Third-party contract review** — at minimum one independent reviewer. Cryptape and a few independent CKB security researchers (e.g. Phoenix in the community) have done lock-script reviews before.
4. **Fee-rate adaptation** — replace SDK-default fee rate with `get_fee_rate_statistics` RPC + a user-settable cap. Today's `completeFeeBy(signer)` will get stuck during congested periods.
5. **Per-owner soft cap in the indexer** — the contract is dust-resistant per packet (every packet pays its own rent), but a single owner can spam thousands of 1-slot packets and bloat the index. Soft cap rather than reject.
6. **Audit-ready relay** — apply the §2.3 fix and log every relayed `tx_hash` for forensics.
7. **Metrics**: tip lag, reorg frequency, claim success rate. Fly.io shared-CPU is fine for testnet but plan an upgrade path before mainnet traffic.
8. **Frontend bundle integrity**: SRI / pinned hashes + public Vercel deploy logs to make "fake frontend, real backend" attacks loud.
9. **Either implement or remove `/v1/messages`** before mainnet — leaving an unauthenticated, unvalidated KV endpoint exposed is a footgun.
10. **Pin and document the mainnet code_hash + cell_dep at deploy time** with `data1` and a `dep_group` containing redundant copies, to defuse the "the one referenced cell got accidentally consumed" failure mode.

**Is the data-layout redesign worth the contract complexity?** Yes — see Q1 above. SMT for `claimed_locks` is the high-leverage change.

**Decentralized sender identity — wallet-level or pckt-shipped primitive?**

**Neither — integrate an existing CKB DID. Specifically: don't ship your own.**

- CKB has [.bit](https://did.id) (formerly DAS) covering a meaningful chunk of mainnet users. Integrating it gives you naming for free and stops fragmenting the CKB naming ecosystem further (.bit, Spore, CKB Alphabet … one more would not help).
- Short-term, the cheapest meaningful upgrade is the wallet-signed attestation in §2.1 (server still stores, but only stores verifiable claims).
- Long-term, layer in .bit / Joy ID identity resolution. If a packet sender is a .bit holder, show the .bit name; otherwise fall back to truncated address. No new primitive.
- If you absolutely must ship a pckt-native primitive, the minimum useful version is a type-script with `args = owner_lock_hash`, `data = utf8(username)`, plus singletonness via outpoint commitment (analogous to Spore cluster IDs). But for any other dApp to adopt it, you'd need schema standardization and wallet support — high coordination cost, low probability of payoff. Don't do it.

**Distribution — where do CKB-native apps actually find users?**

- **Demo → first 100 users**: Nervos Community Catalyst (this org), Nervos Discord dApp channels, @CKBcommunity on Twitter/X, Zhihu Nervos topic. These users are tech-curious, willing to use testnet, and give good feedback — but they're not "send red packets daily" users.
- **→ first 1000 users**: integrate with wallets that have dApp browsers. **Joy ID inclusion is the fastest path** — they have a low integration bar for utility dApps and a meaningful active user base.
- **→ break out**: tie a release to a CKB-native event (e.g. Lunar New Year, ecosystem anniversary). This is exactly what your planned "Group / event mode" is shaped for. Bitcoin's ordinals/runes red-packet activations have moved real volume; CKB has no equivalent slot, and pckt + a Spore NFT collab could occupy it.
- **Don't chase non-crypto mass adoption yet.** WeChat-red-packet users won't bridge to CKB on their own. The realistic positioning is "the default tool for sending red packets *within the CKB community*" first, then expand outward. Trying to skip step 1 burns you out.

---

## TL;DR — Three things that matter most

1. **Before mainnet**: validate `script_hash(address) == owner_lock_hash` on profile upsert (§2.1), make the relay packet-only (§2.3), and make reorg rollback rebuild from per-outpoint history rather than blanket-deleting (§2.2).
2. **Worth doing**: SMT for `claimed_locks`. Floor drops from ~185 CKB to ~30 CKB — that *is* the product.
3. **Avoid the temptation to**: ship your own DID. Integrate .bit + signed-attestation profiles, get 90% of the value for 10% of the work.

The contract layer is meaningfully better than the average CKB dApp — successor uniqueness, strict `since` whitelisting, recipient cell-data rejection are all correctly handled. The remaining gaps are all in the backend trust boundary, and those are far cheaper to fix than the contract-level work you've already done. Nice project.

issueThreads.body: **Project Summary:** CKB Escrow is a standalone decentralized escrow app for goods and services between known parties on Nervos CKB. A buyer can create and fund an escrow for a known seller, the seller can mark the work or goods as delivered, the buyer can release funds or open a dispute, and an arbitrator can resolve disputed escrows to either party. The project is not a marketplace or storefront; it focuses on the escrow workflow itself, with wallet-first identity, role-aware actions, indexer-backed escrow history, and a product UI supported by a separate protocol/studio interface. **Tools used:** - Rust for CKB script development - CKB RISC-V VM contract model - `ckb-std` - `ckb-testtool` - Docker reproducible contract builds - `@offckb/cli` for deployment tooling - CCC / CKB wallet integration - TypeScript - Next.js - React - Tailwind CSS - shadcn-style UI primitives - Postgres-ready escrow indexer storage - Neon/Postgres planned for hosted production history - Vercel planned for frontend hosting **Current features:** - Buyer-first escrow product UI - Wallet-first identity, no email/password registration - Testnet/mainnet network selection in the frontend - Buyer can create and fund escrow for a known seller - Seller can discover escrows they belong to and mark delivered - Buyer can release funds, cancel where allowed, dispute, or refund after deadline - Arbitrator can review disputed escrows and resolve to buyer or seller - Role-aware escrow discovery for buyer, seller, and arbitrator - Active and past escrow views - Terminal escrow history through indexer-backed recovery design - Escrow detail “deal room” with timeline, status, parties, actions, and receipt mode - Dispute evidence flow using off-chain evidence metadata and hashes - `/studio` route for protocol/debug/deployment workflows - Contract documentation, frontend documentation, and deployment notes - Reproducible build/checksum workflow for the contract - OffCKB deployment tooling support **Planned features:** - Complete full hosted testnet end-to-end validation: - buyer creates and funds escrow - seller marks delivered - buyer releases funds - buyer cancels before delivery - buyer refunds after deadline - buyer/seller opens dispute - arbitrator resolves to buyer or seller - Improve the hosted indexer so escrow history syncs continuously instead of only through API-triggered scans. - Connect production Postgres/Neon for reliable cross-device escrow history. - comments.author: Officeyutong
comments.body:
After reviewing both the [contract repository](https://github.com/kayceeDev/ckb-escrow) and the [frontend repository](https://github.com/kayceeDev/ckb-escrow-studio), the overall architecture is viable on CKB. The cell-based state machine, CCC transaction layer, role-aware UI, indexer package, PostgreSQL schema, and separate /studio interface are good foundations.
Before public testnet testing, I recommend addressing these issues:

## Terminal payout validation can be bypassed.

The contract checks only whether the recipient’s total output capacity is at least amount; it does not subtract capacity already supplied by the recipient’s own inputs. An attacker could satisfy the apparent payout using another input while redirecting escrow capacity elsewhere. See [main.rs#L146-L185](https://github.com/kayceeDev/ckb-escrow/blob/36d1d189ee3b8868f8f38beda1622875ca2b8dc2/contracts/escrow-lock/src/main.rs#L146-L185).
The CCC adapter builds the intended settlement correctly by sending the escrow cell capacity to the recipient ([transactions.ts#L186-L221](https://github.com/kayceeDev/ckb-escrow-studio/blob/854039ca7a520615a4a75bbb084289f11ed31c1e/packages/ccc-adapter/src/transactions.ts#L186-L221)), but contract security must not depend on the frontend builder.

## Dispute APIs have no cryptographic authorization.

The API accepts openedByLockHash, submittedByLockHash, and decidedByLockHash directly from the request body without a wallet signature or authenticated session. See [dispute/route.ts#L81-L130](https://github.com/kayceeDev/ckb-escrow-studio/blob/854039ca7a520615a4a75bbb084289f11ed31c1e/packages/frontend/app/api/escrows/%5Bid%5D/dispute/route.ts#L81-L130).
Storage verifies that the supplied hash belongs to the expected role ([postgres.ts#L561-L637](https://github.com/kayceeDev/ckb-escrow-studio/blob/854039ca7a520615a4a75bbb084289f11ed31c1e/packages/escrow-indexer/src/postgres.ts#L561-L637)), but anyone can copy a public participant hash. Require a nonce and wallet signature, and verify that submitted dispute/resolution transaction hashes exist on-chain and match the escrow and action.


The UX and /studio separation are appropriate: product actions are role- and state-aware, while protocol details remain secondary. For CCC, continue verifying full recipient lock scripts, deployment metadata, CellDeps, fees, change, network/genesis, and current outpoint status immediately before signing.
Mainnet should remain gated until the payout vulnerability and dispute API authentication are fixed, all integration tests and real testnet flows pass, indexer reorganization recovery is demonstrated, reproducible deployment metadata is verified, and the contract receives an independent security review.

comments.author: Xcodes-chain
comments.body:
I completed a combined acceptance review of the live testnet deployment, the current repository at commit `94bea5cfd62ab4960109dbe8f819d032e062dade`, and the local acceptance observations recorded in `nervosnetwork/acceptance-internal#1610`.

## Acceptance result

**Result: accepted as a testnet POC; not ready for mainnet.**

What was verified:

- The production UI, REST API, WebSocket market data, order book, recent trades, and xUDT faucet health endpoint are reachable.
- Live orders resolve to unspent CKB testnet cells, and a sampled recent trade (`0xb038...b3af`) is committed on-chain.
- The deployed DEX binary hash matches the checked-in testnet deployment registry (`0x8560...df3b`). The contract suite passed **20/20** against that deployed binary.
- UI lint/build, backend build, off-chain type checks, and faucet build passed. Seven non-bot backend tests passed. The full backend test command is currently blocked by a stale DEX code-hash fixture in `backend/src/bot/index.test.ts`, rather than a runtime failure.
- The local wallet flow could place a limit order. The observed UX issues are: balance refresh takes about 1–2 seconds, opening the wallet for signing takes about 3 seconds, and there is no direct link to the CKB testnet faucet.
- The UI exposes a Market tab, but submitting a market order is intentionally rejected. This should be hidden or clearly labelled as unavailable.
- The planned AMM is not implemented/usable yet. The present matcher only fills an exact pair with the same xUDT type hash, token amount, and total price; a crossing limit price alone does not guarantee execution.

The current source could not be rebuilt to RISC-V on the Apple host used for this review because the available clang has no RISC-V backend and Docker was unavailable. This limits source-to-binary reproducibility evidence, although the downloaded deployed binary matched the deployment record and passed the contract tests.

## Answers to the feedback questions

1. **Is the order-cell and settlement design sound?**  
   The core POC idea is sound: orders live in CKB cells, matching is off-chain, and settlement invariants are checked on-chain. The current contract correctly checks exact token amount/price pairs and the principal seller/buyer outputs for a complete fill. Before production, cancellation must also enforce a canonical maker refund output, and BID settlement must explicitly conserve/refund capacity or cap the matcher fee. At present, the cancellation branch proves a maker-hash input exists but does not validate where the order value goes, while a BID's capacity is only lower-bounded.

2. **Security issues and edge cases before mainnet?**  
   The main priorities are: fail closed when the internal ingestion token is absent/default; verify ingested events against CKB rather than treating event payloads as chain truth; make ingestion writes truly atomic; add fork-aware indexing with block-hash checkpoints and confirmation depth; prevent one invalid exact-match pair from stalling the reference matcher; bind `CKB_NETWORK`, RPC genesis, client type, xUDT deps, and DEX deps to one deployment manifest; add WebSocket/API bounds and database-side pagination; and keep the faucet testnet-only with atomic claims and global budgets. The transaction contract also needs explicit cancellation-refund and BID-surplus invariants. My repository-wide review found **1 high and 8 medium** items across these areas.

3. **Is a permissionless trading bot practical?**  
   Technically yes: it fits CKB because the bot does not need custody or a signing key when the lock script fully defines a valid settlement. Economically and operationally it is incomplete. Define a bounded matcher reward, deterministic selection/priority rules, failed-pair quarantine, replacement/race handling, reorg behavior, and a standard discovery/config format so independent bots can interoperate.

4. **Recommended partial-fill design?**  
   Consume the old order cell and create one canonical successor order cell. Keep maker, pair, side, limit price, nonce/version, and policy immutable; reduce `remaining_base`/`remaining_quote` exactly. The lock should enforce conservation, price inequality, deterministic rounding, minimum fill/dust rules, fee/refund caps, and successor output position/type/data. Cancellation then consumes the latest successor. This is safer than mutable off-chain fill accounting.

5. **CKB-specific patterns/primitives?**  
   Continue using [xUDT](https://github.com/nervosnetwork/rfcs/blob/master/rfcs/0052-extensible-udt/0052-extensible-udt.md), and study [CoBuild](https://talk.nervos.org/t/ckb-transaction-cobuild-protocol-overview/7702) / Open Transaction patterns for composing user intent with third-party matching. Use `since` where an expiry/refund policy benefits from a time bound, and publish an immutable deployment manifest that pins code hashes, hash types, deps, network genesis, and supported assets. Capacity and cell-dep accounting should be part of the protocol specification, not only client behavior.

6. **What would I change for mainnet?**  
   Make the chain the rebuildable source of truth; separate the public API, indexer, and matcher failure domains; persist fork-aware checkpoints; run multiple stateless permissionless matchers; define an allowlisted market/deployment registry; add transaction simulation and human-readable wallet intent; produce reproducible contract builds with signed/checksummed artifacts; and commission an independent contract audit after the protocol invariants stabilize.

7. **Projects/standards to study?**  
   [UTXOSwap](https://utxoswap.gitbook.io/en) is the closest reference for CKB intent cells, off-chain matching, on-chain verification, Open Transactions, and AMM design. Also study the xUDT RFC and CoBuild above. [YokaiSwap](https://docs.yokaiswap.com/products/exchange) is useful as a product/economic comparison, although its exchange is an L2 EVM AMM rather than this L1 cell-based order book.

8. **Main technical limitations?**  
   Current matching is exact-only, one BID plus one ASK per settlement, with no ordinary crossing-price execution, partial fills, market orders, or usable AMM liquidity. Every order consumes L1 capacity and creates UTXO fragmentation; confirmation latency and reorgs affect UX; public matching creates races; and without an explicit reward, independent bot operation has weak incentives. Large public books also require indexed server-side pagination instead of in-process sorting/snapshots.

9. **Does this fit CKB DeFi?**  
   Yes. Off-chain discovery/construction plus on-chain verification maps well to CKB's cell model and keeps custody in scripts. The trade-off is that putting every order cell on L1 carries capacity, fragmentation, latency, and throughput costs. The protocol should therefore keep the on-chain intent compact and make execution composable.

10. **Biggest missing piece?**  
    A written, versioned protocol specification with invariant-complete contract enforcement. It should define partial/crossing fills, cancellation refunds, capacity/fee ownership, rounding/dust, bot rewards, race/reorg semantics, network/deployment identity, and compatibility rules. Once that exists, the clients, bots, tests, documentation, and audit can all target the same protocol instead of relying on reference-client behavior.

## Suggested acceptance follow-ups

1. Add an obvious CKB testnet faucet link and explicit loading states for balance refresh and wallet wake-up.
2. Hide/disable the Market tab and AMM presentation until implemented, or label both as planned.
3. Update the contract README and `offchain/src/fill-order.ts`; they still describe/parse the old 40-byte ASK-only format while the current contract uses a versioned 90-byte BID/ASK format.
4. Fix the stale backend bot test fixture so the default test command is green.
5. Resolve the contract invariants and chain/indexer safety items above before adding partial fills, because partial fills multiply those edge cases.

issueThreads.title: Cells (cellula.id): .cell names on CKB that can be paid, contracts public and reproducible
issueThreads.author: LusoCryptoLabs
issueThreads.body:
**Project Summary:** Cells is a permissionless naming protocol on CKB. A `.cell` name is one live cell under a fixed type script; its records ride in the witness and the cell commits to their hash. What it adds over a lookup: the name can be paid. It publishes addresses per chain, a Lightning Address (`name@cellula.id`, forwarded unchanged to the wallet the name publishes), a Fiber node endpoint, and signed payment requests that carry bank details (SEPA, Pix, UPI) without putting them on chain. Ownership is a lock hash in the cell's data, proven by co-spending a cell under that lock, so any lock CKB has or gets later works without a release. Live on mainnet since 21 September 2026.

**Tools used:** `ckb-std` and `ckb-testtool` for the four scripts (Rust, reproducible builds); `@ckb-ccc/core` and `@ckb-ccc/connector-react` for the SDK and the app (JoyID, MetaMask, OKX, UniSat, UTXO Global); the `AddressResolver` hook in `@ckb-ccc/core` 1.23.0, which we contributed (ckb-devrel/ccc#575); `ckbfs` for the app's own bytes on chain; `@noble/post-quantum` for the SPHINCS+ owner path; `fnn` for the Fiber payment tests on testnet.

**Current features:**
- Permissionless registration with commit-reveal enforced by the type script, and a predecessor preserved byte for byte except its `next` pointer.
- Records with a published layout, addresses per SLIP-44 coin, Lightning Address forwarding, Fiber endpoint, avatar and cover in the witness.
- Signed payment requests in CKB, sats, EUR, BRL, INR and USDC on three chains.
- Owner and manager split, sub-names (a fifth of the parent's fee), transfer, and a sale lock with the fee fixed in the contract.
- A post-quantum owner through `sphincs-all-in-one-lock`, live on mainnet.
- A public read API with a proof in every answer, sign-in with a name, `/verify` against the published build, and the app's own bytes on chain.
- A `.cell` resolver for CCC's `AddressResolver`: an app built on CCC accepts `.cell` names in `Address.fromString` with one line, each answer checked against the app's own client. Ships in the next `cellula-sdk` release.
- Indexed by ckbadger (janx/ckbadger#14).

**Planned features:**
- Publish the CCC resolver in `cellula-sdk`, then integrations with apps that take CKB addresses.
- Names held as a deed (a Spore), live on testnet, on mainnet once its cluster exists.
- Constrain the upgrade key (single key today, stated in `TRUST.md`).
- A second, independently run resolver.

**Deployed on:** Mainnet (`cellula.id`, since 2026-09-21, 62 names, most of them the reserved set) and testnet (`testnet.cellula.id`, free names).

**Link to repository:** contracts https://github.com/LusoCryptoLabs/cells-contracts (CI rebuilds the mainnet binaries and compares their hashes); resolver https://github.com/LusoCryptoLabs/cells-resolver; bug classes met on the way, https://github.com/LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-script-pitfalls. The app's source is private for now. Milestones: https://github.com/LusoCryptoLabs/cells-contracts/blob/main/MILESTONES.md

**Link to hosted version of project:** https://cellula.id (mainnet), https://testnet.cellula.id (free to try), developers: https://cellula.id/developers

**Request for feedback:**
- **Problems:** none blocking. One open ask elsewhere: script labels on the explorer (`ckb-explorer-frontend#2140`).
- **Review:** authorization is delegated to the owner's lock: an owner action needs any input under the owner's lock hash, and the contract refuses only its own always-success lock. A lock that lets a third party spend its cells, such as anyone-can-pay or Omnilock in ACP mode, would therefore let anyone act as the owner. We plan to refuse such locks as owners in the SDK rather than in the contract. Which lock code hashes and flags would you put on that list?
- **Guidance:** for builders whose apps take a CKB address, would you accept `.cell` names there through the CCC resolver, and what is missing before you would?

Product story and technical detail: https://talk.nervos.org/t/cellula-id-cell-names-on-ckb-with-the-contracts-public-and-reproducible/10753

issueThreads.title: EventMesh: bilateral signed reconciliation for CKB/Fiber application events
issueThreads.author: tydeptrai21042004
issueThreads.body: ## Project Summary EventMesh is a bilateral reconciliation layer for applications using CKB and Fiber where two independently operated systems may disagree about the application state associated with a payment after a timeout, retry, crash, lost response, or restart. Instead of treating a sender-side payment-success response as sufficient proof, EventMesh records a signed, hash-linked application transcript between two operators, requires explicit acknowledgement of exact events, can bind receiver-verified Fiber payment evidence to the transcript, and lets both operators sign the same final commitment. That commitment can then optionally be checkpointed to CKB. EventMesh is intended to complement Fiber rather than replace it: **Fiber answers whether value moved, while EventMesh records which application state both operators accepted.** ## Tools used - TypeScript - Node.js 22 - React 19 - Vite 7 - `@ckb-ccc/shell` for CKB integration - Fiber JSON-RPC integration - `@noble/curves` for secp256k1 cryptography - Fastify - Zod - Vitest - Vercel serverless deployment - CKB Testnet RPC - SHA-256 hash-linked transcripts and deterministic commitments - No Postgres / Neon / Blob / SQLite dependency for the Vercel preview ## Current features - Two distinct operator identities: requester/payer and provider/receiver. - Signed bilateral sessions with bounded expiration. - Domain-separated secp256k1 signatures for sessions, events, acknowledgements, and final commitments. - Hash-linked event transcript using previous-hash references. - Explicit ACK/REJECT of exact signed event hashes. - Service reconciliation state machine: 1. request service; 2. accept request; 3. commit result; 4. complete service; 5. close with dual signatures. - Deterministic final-state commitment. - Dual-signed close proving both operators agreed to the same final transcript. - Portable JSON evidence export. - Portable verifier for session signatures, event signatures, hashes, chain links, acknowledgements, and final commitments. - Import and recovery of previously exported signed evidence. - Optimistic concurrency protection using expected event count and expected chain tip. - Rejection of stale writes and detection of competing/forked descendants. - Short browser edit lease to reduce accidental same-browser concurrent edits. - Strict event allow-list and service-flow validation. - Bounded payload, session TTL, event-count, result-size, and final-state limits. - Separate **Demo** and **Real / Testnet** workspaces. - Deterministic server-side demo identities. - Demo session recovery from signed browser snapshots after Vercel/serverless cold starts. - Demo CKB broadcasting intentionally disabled. - Real / Testnet access protected by an access key kept in browser memory rather than Local Storage. - Server-side Testnet operator identities. - CKB Testnet RPC readiness checks. - Optional receiver-side Fiber verification. - `PAYMENT_SETTLED` fails closed unless the receiver-side Fiber node verifies the payment. - Optional CKB commitment/checkpoint support. - CKB transaction identity determined before broadcast so ambiguous broadcast results can be recovered by transaction hash rather than blindly resubmitted. - Deployment diagnostics and health checks. - Automated unit/integration tests and deployment verification scripts. - One-project Vercel deployment for the reference/demo interface. ## Planned features - Run Operator A and Operator B as genuinely independent services with independent durable storage. - Complete a reproducible end-to-end Fiber Testnet payment flow using separate Fiber nodes. - Enable receiver-owned Fiber payment verification in the public Testnet reference deployment. - Enable an explicitly controlled CKB Testnet checkpoint transaction and show pending -> committed -> confirmed lifecycle. - Publish a complete evidence package containing signed EventMesh transcript, Fiber payment hash, receiver verification evidence, CKB transaction hash, and independent verification instructions. - Integrate EventMesh into an external CKB/Fiber application through the adapter SDK. - Expand failure/recovery testing for lost responses, retries, crashes, cold starts, duplicate delivery, stale clients, and divergent operator state. - Investigate batching multiple session commitments into a higher-level CKB commitment. - Improve the production deployment model beyond the database-free serverless preview. - Resolve the public project-name collision with Apache EventMesh before a wider production launch. ## Deployed on **CKB Testnet / preview** The current public deployment has two distinct modes. ### Demo - Fully usable for the signed reconciliation walkthrough. - Uses deterministic preview identities. - Does not use production funds. - Does not broadcast CKB transactions. - Does not require a database. ### Real / Testnet - Supports configured Testnet operator identities and integrations. - CKB Testnet RPC connectivity is available. - Mutations require an explicit access gate. - Automatic flows are disabled; state transitions are manual. - The current hosted deployment reports that Testnet operator-security configuration is incomplete. - Receiver-side Fiber RPC is currently optional/not configured in the hosted instance. - CKB broadcasting is off by default and is not presented as enabled in the current hosted preview. Therefore the hosted version should currently be described as a **Testnet reference/validation deployment**, not production custody infrastructure. ## Link to repository https://github.com/tydeptrai21042004/eventmesh ## Link to hosted version https://eventmesh-tan.vercel.app/ ## Screenshots ### Demo workspace The Demo workspace exposes the complete signed reconciliation walkthrough without requiring funds or external infrastructure. ### Signed state-machine workflow This view exposes the session ID, operator identities, current chain tip, event count, explicit state transitions, portable verification, and stale-write/fork protection. ## Request for feedback ### Problems #### 1. Is the reconciliation problem real/useful for CKB/Fiber applications? The project starts from the case where a Fiber payment succeeds but two independently operated applications can still disagree about which application event or result that payment settled after a timeout, crash, retry, or lost response. I would like feedback on whether CKB/Fiber builders encounter this class of problem in practice and whether a bilateral reconciliation layer is a useful abstraction. #### 2. Is the separation between Fiber, EventMesh, and CKB sensible? The current model is approximately: ```text Fiber: prove/observe that value moved EventMesh: prove which application event/state both operators accepted CKB: optionally provide a durable compact checkpoint of that agreement ``` I would like reviewers to challenge this separation and identify cases where responsibilities are duplicated, missing, or placed at the wrong layer. #### 3. Is receiver-side Fiber verification the correct trust boundary? EventMesh intentionally does not accept a sender assertion such as "my payment RPC returned success" as sufficient evidence for `PAYMENT_SETTLED`. The receiving operator must independently query its Fiber node and verify the matching payment/invoice before acknowledging the settlement event. I would appreciate feedback on whether this is the correct Fiber integration pattern and whether additional Fiber-specific evidence should be committed into the transcript. #### 4. Is the signed transcript/state-machine design sufficient? I would like review of: - domain-separated signatures; - hash-linked events; - exact ACK/REJECT semantics; - previous-hash preconditions; - event-count preconditions; - duplicate/idempotent delivery; - dual-signed final state; - stale-write handling; - fork detection; - portable evidence verification. In particular, I would appreciate examples of adversarial or failure cases that the current protocol still handles incorrectly. #### 5. Is the CKB commitment useful and minimal? The intention is not to write every event to CKB. EventMesh instead creates a compact commitment to the bilateral proof and can checkpoint that commitment after the two operators agree. I would appreciate feedback on: - whether CKB is being used appropriately here; - what should be included in the commitment; - whether per-session anchoring is reasonable for the validation stage; - when batching commitments would become preferable. #### 6. Database-free serverless limitation The Vercel reference deployment deliberately avoids a shared database. Signed snapshots plus optimistic chain preconditions make stale or conflicting state detectable, but they cannot provide a globally serialized lock across independent Vercel instances. Two clients starting from exactly the same valid snapshot could therefore create different next events on different cold instances. Both branches can be cryptographically valid, although the fork is detectable. For production I currently expect Operator A and Operator B to run as independent services with durable operator-owned state. I would appreciate feedback on whether this separation between the lightweight public demo and the intended production architecture is reasonable. ### Review I would like CKBuilders reviewers to review: - whether the core concept fills a useful gap around CKB/Fiber application coordination; - whether the protocol has unnecessary complexity; - whether important replay, equivocation, crash-recovery, or retry cases are missing; - whether the Fiber verification model is correct; - whether the CKB checkpoint design makes sense; - whether the adapter boundary is suitable for integration by other applications; - whether there are existing CKB/Fiber projects or primitives with which EventMesh overlaps and should integrate instead of reimplementing; - what would need to change before this could move from a Testnet reference implementation toward a production-capable system. ### Guidance The main guidance I am looking for is what the next validation milestone should be. My current proposed milestone is: ```text independent Operator A | | signed application event v independent Operator B | | receiver-verified real Fiber Testnet payment v dual-signed EventMesh close | | compact commitment v CKB Testnet transaction | v independent transcript + Fiber + CKB verification ``` I would especially appreciate advice on whether this is the right next proof, what evidence CKBuilders would expect from it, and which parts of the protocol should be simplified or strengthened before adding more features.

comments.body:
Fiber already covers normal business binding. A merchant creates an invoice and keeps payment_hash ↔ order in its own DB; it can put an order reference in description, and the payer can attach custom_records (final hop only, ~2KB,
 keys 0–65535) carrying order/user/correlation IDs. After payment, the merchant queries the invoice by payment_hash and gets a definitive Paid/preimage result. For most payment flows, that is enough to bind a payment to a business object and let Fiber adjudicate whether value moved.

The limit is that this is unilateral metadata, not a bilateral signed application state: it proves which invoice was paid, not that both operators accepted the same service result.

For this project, I'm not sure the whether there is a real demand for it:
in which concrete scenarios is that not enough? Could you describe 2–3 cases, with (a) who A and B are, (b) what is paid for, (c) what exactly they disagree about after a timeout/retry/crash, and (d) why an
 invoice reference + idempotent API + shared DB/contract cannot resolve it? If both sides trust Fiber for settlement, is the remaining gap really a protocol problem rather than a delivery/contract problem?

comments.author: chenyukang
comments.body: Fiber/Lightning solve a strong version of "bilateral agreement": two parties agree on channel state, with collateral locked in the channel, commitment transactions, revocation/punishment, and on-chain enforcement when they disagree. EventMesh looks similar but is a different strength class — it records what two keys signed; it does not enforce or resolve disagreement.

issueThreads.title: FreightOnNervos (FON) or Freight43: a CKB-native deliverables network, open for feedback
issueThreads.author: Birdmannn
issueThreads.body:
## Project Summary

Freight on Nervos (FON) is a social application for creating, funding, participating in, and delivering "freights": work, gifts, and raffles with explicit rules for who may participate and when value can be released. **Every proposed transaction can be a deliverable.** A freight can be a simple post that someone tips, a funded task with a defined recipient, a giveaway with verifiable winner selection, or a task whose eligibility depends on actions in another app.

The aim is to let a creator state the work and its conditions, let other people contribute funds or participate, and make the important money-moving rules enforceable by a CKB script. The social layer and external-app verification live in FON's web application; they are not presented as on-chain facts when they are not. This is a live testnet demo, not a claim that every edge case is finished or audited.

## Tools Used

- **CKB and Rust:** a freight type script for campaign state, escrow transitions, raffle settlement, approvals, and gift-claim rules.
- **CCC and JoyID:** wallet connection and signing; the Checkbox Demo also uses JoyID so its activity belongs to a connected CKB address.
- **Next.js, React, and TypeScript:** the FON interface, API, SDK integration, and separately deployed demo app.
- **MongoDB:** profiles, freight metadata, registered mountable apps, off-chain participation and completion, and demo state.
- **FON SDK and webhooks:** the server-side integration surface through which hosted apps register principles and exchange freight events.

## Current Features

### Freights, funding, and tipping

FON has simple tasks, funded tasks/gifts, crowdfunding and timed-challenge types, ordinary raffles, and recurring raffles. Creators can write a post, add images, set the relevant timing and funding arguments, attach conditions, save a draft, preview it, and publish through their wallet. Participants can discover the freight from the feed or profiles, inspect its conditions, and take the actions appropriate to its type.

**Tipping is available on ordinary freights.** A simple task can serve as a continuing piece of work or a creator's open-ended post: it displays as ongoing rather than expiring like a timed raffle. A supporter can send CKB as appreciation; for simple tasks, the tip transaction pays the creator's wallet directly and records the support on the freight. Other freight types can accept deposits into their campaign balance, subject to their state and rules. That distinction matters: a direct creator tip is not a promise that the supporter has bought a raffle ticket or acquired a claim on escrow.

**Funded gifts and claims** let a creator describe a deliverable and fund an allocation for eligible claimants. The current gift policy fixes claim slots and amounts at creation, supports open or tagged claimants and equal or ratio-based splits, and pays a claimant through a wallet-signed on-chain transaction. The contract checks the claimant and available escrow, rather than treating an editable database record as payment authority. Funding and delivery can also be subject to an approval gate. This can model a funded proposal: contributors provide the resources, a creator performs the work, and named inspectors approve commencement before claims or release proceed. The recipient may be designated with `@claim`; unsupported streaming through `@receive` is deliberately not presented as a working feature.

### Raffles and verifiable selection

In an **ordinary raffle**, users obtain tickets during the entry window. Paid tickets fund the raffle pool; free-entry raffles need other funding. Voluntary support deposits can also contribute a creator-selected percentage to the winners' pool, with the remainder kept separate for creator withdrawal under the freight's rules. A purchase can contain multiple tickets, each represented as a separate participant entry and therefore another chance in the draw. The creator sets the number of winners and a tickets-per-wallet limit. The app checks prior entries before allowing another purchase, while the current contract enforces the ticket quantity per transaction; whether the cumulative wallet limit should also be enforced on-chain is an important review question. If eligible participant entries do not exceed the winner count, everyone can win; otherwise the winning entries must be selected.

The randomness path uses **commit, reveal, and deterministic selection**. The creator commits a hash of a secret value when creating the raffle. At settlement, the preimage is revealed and the contract verifies that its Blake2b hash matches the stored commitment. Eligible participant cells are put in a canonical order using join time, address, and input outpoint as tie-breakers. The revealed value, campaign identity, and participant count derive a seed; a deterministic Fisher-Yates shuffle with rejection sampling selects the first required entries. The contract checks the proposed winner outputs and equal per-winner amount against that result. This gives reviewers concrete inputs to reproduce and challenge a draw; it does **not** remove the need to examine creator withholding of the reveal, ticket accounting, or the complete settlement UX.

**Recurring raffles** turn one raffle into rounds. Participants buy into an active round; when it closes, an on-chain draw marks winners and non-winners without immediately paying everybody. The freight enters a creator-configured sleep period. Winners can cash out during that window; non-winners are eliminated from that round. When sleep ends, unclaimed value remains in the pool, the next winner count is reduced by the configured percentage (never below one), and a new round starts. New or previous users can buy tickets for that next round as new entries. The process ends when a round has one winner, whether that winner cashes out during sleep or the final round closes. The round number, winner count, claimable amounts, pool, and transitions are represented in campaign/participant state and checked by the contract. It is a different product from a one-shot giveaway: each sleep period is a real choice between taking a known claim and continuing the competition.

This recurring flow is **implemented and its automated tests pass**, but it has not been established as error-free in real use. Meaningful end-to-end testing needs more independent participants and wallets across several rounds, especially around cash-out, non-claims, and rollover. So far I have been testing mostly alone with at most three wallets, which also means juggling three browser sessions; I have not had enough test users to exercise it at realistic scale. I would particularly welcome people willing to test these transitions and report failures.

### Mountables: freight conditions and delivery signals

**All freight constraints are treated as mountables, but not all mountables are constraints.** Some built-in mounted signals describe how a freight behaves, such as being rewardable or requiring a signature; others actively gate participation or completion. A creator can select multiple conditions, and all required conditions must be satisfied before FON marks the same wallet canonically complete. This creates a useful exchange: the creator can narrow eligibility to people who performed the requested work, while participants can demonstrate that work and compete for or claim the associated value. On a funded freight, additional supporters can contribute to the pool without needing to be the original creator.

The main extensibility point is a **mounted app**. Any hosted app can use the FON SDK to register its logo, endpoints, and a catalogue of principles. Each principle has a title, explanation, parameter schema, and a true/false evaluation for a participant. For example, a reputation app could expose `reputation-greater-than` with a numeric parameter. A creator could mount it with `10000`, making a reputation above that number one of the freight's required conditions. That is an illustration of the SDK, not a claim that this particular reputation app is already integrated. The live Checkbox Demo instead exposes checkbox, checkbox-count, checkbox-set, and exact-text principles. A creator can set the exact word; a participant must enter that word in the demo to satisfy the selected principle.

Registration is app-level, not per freight. At setup, FON asks the hosted app to verify the selected principle configuration. After publication gives the freight its final ID, FON sends an authenticated `mount.requested` webhook containing that ID, selected principles and parameters, start/end times, duration in seconds, FON's event URL, and a **freight-scoped secret**. The app may push participant states during that window; FON rejects updates outside it and recalculates completion. An optional polling fallback exists, but is disabled by default and needs a separately configured worker. The app-registration secret and each freight's expiring event secret serve different purposes, and neither belongs in browser code.

**FBARS locks** are a built-in participation condition. FBARS are FON's current participation/reputation points, awarded for qualifying wallet, funding, social, and reward activity; they are not yet a mintable token. A creator can block participants *below* a chosen FBARS threshold or block those *at or above* it. Someone with at least **5 times the creator's current FBARS** can bypass that lock. This deliberately lets a creator target a particular participation band without making the lock absolute against a substantially more established account. FBARS also drive weekly/overall rankings; the weekly leader can edit the public marquee within a limited weekly allowance.

**Child Freight** is another built-in condition. A creator can require a participant to publish a direct child freight, optionally with a specified title, before the original freight counts that participant as complete. Separately, published freights can be linked for tracking without making the link a completion requirement. A future lightweight "ref" is intended to make that reference-only use even clearer in the UI.

**Parent and child relationships** give freights a dependency graph. A child can have multiple direct parents; the same participant must clear the child's own conditions and its ancestors' conditions before current completion is granted. The creator can attach parents, while another creator may **encroach** by attaching a freight they own as a parent only if they hold at least **10 times the child's creator's current FBARS** at that moment. The relationship rejects cycles and redundant "absolute" links, and the tree can be inspected from Freight Options. Adding a new head parent re-evaluates completion throughout its descendants. It does **not** reverse CKB rewards that were already paid: past settlement is historical, while current off-chain completion can become pending for future interactions.

**Signable/approval gates** are shown as mounted signals even though they are not chosen from the ordinary app catalogue. Tagged `@approve` wallets approve with signed CKB transactions. Ordinary raffles may require approvals before commencement (all or a threshold, before the start-delay deadline) or unanimous approval before delivery; recurring raffles support the initial commencement gate. Gift freights support a commencement approval gate, including all/threshold quorum, before claims and release. The contract stores approver lock hashes and approval state, and checks the relevant transition instead of trusting only a UI badge. This is useful when funders want an inspector's consent before a funded deliverable proceeds. It is important not to conflate the stages: **on-delivery approval is currently an ordinary-raffle option, while the implemented gift gate is on commencement**.

The code also contains a Google Forms verification path, but **Forms is currently disabled in the mountable chooser**. I do not want reviewers to mistake its presence in the repo for a ready-to-select live integration. Rewardable and signable icons on freight cards are likewise indicators of behavior, not separate third-party apps.

### Social context and transparency

FON includes profiles, a freight feed, comments, likes, reshares, quote/reference actions, photos, wallet-linked activity, and weekly/overall leaderboards. Profiles also calculate an ADSF metric from verified reward payouts, direct tips, and gift claims. Freight cards surface status, type, time remaining, creator identity, and mounted-condition indicators; the detail view exposes participation and financial actions. The separately hosted Checkbox Demo has a visible log of registration, inbound FON webhooks, outbound participant updates, and responses, with secret fields redacted. These interfaces are meant to make a freight's rules and its integration behavior inspectable, not just to hide them behind a final "success" label.

## How to Use (The Flow and How to Test)

### As a FON user

1. Open the testnet FON app and connect a CKB wallet. Obtain testnet CKB before attempting transactions that need capacity, fees, tickets, or funding.
2. Create a freight with a title and body. Choose the freight type with its first hashtag, then set its timing, funding, ticket, or gift parameters. Add `#mounted` to open the mountable chooser. Select built-in conditions and/or the registered Checkbox Demo, configure the desired principles, and review the resulting freight before signing and publishing.
3. Other users can inspect the freight and its mounted conditions. Where allowed, they can tip, deposit, buy tickets, approve, claim, or complete the task. The app evaluates the appropriate conditions for their own wallet before treating them as complete or eligible.
4. For a raffle, let the entry window close and inspect the draw and settlement actions. For a recurring raffle, inspect the sleep/cash-out period and next round. For a connected freight family, use **Freight Options > View tree** to see dependencies.

### Test FON with the live Checkbox Demo

1. In FON, publish a testnet freight with `#mounted` and select **FON Checkbox Demo**. Choose at least one principle, such as a checkbox or **Exact Text Match** with your chosen word. Give the freight enough active time to complete the test.
2. Open the separately hosted Checkbox Demo and connect **the same JoyID wallet address** used in FON. Check the required boxes or enter the exact word. A different address is a different participant.
3. Watch the demo's **Logs** to distinguish FON-to-demo mount/activity requests from demo-to-FON event updates and FON's responses. Return to the freight to inspect whether its selected principles and overall completion changed. Expired mount credentials should no longer authorize new updates.

### As a developer integrating an app

1. Deploy a backend with a public logo and the SDK endpoints for mount verification and activity webhooks. Define a manifest containing a stable `appId`, app metadata, and principle definitions with their parameter schemas.
2. From trusted server-side code, call `registerWithFon(fonUrl, manifest)` **once**. Keep the returned registration credential private; provide it only for later authenticated manifest updates and for verifying FON's calls. The live Checkbox Demo in the repository is a concrete Next.js implementation of this flow.
3. When FON calls your verification endpoint, validate the creator's selected principles and parameters. When FON later calls your activity webhook with `mount.requested`, persist the freight-specific URL, secret, principles, and active window on your backend.
4. Evaluate participant activity against those selected principles and send true/false states to FON during the allowed window. Do not send the app or freight secret to the participant's browser. Consult the repo's `MOUNT_FLOW.md` for payloads and trust boundaries.

First-time third-party registration currently needs stronger ownership verification before it should be opened as unrestricted self-service; that is called out below rather than concealed by the demo.

## Planned Features

- **Secure developer onboarding.** Authenticate who owns an app registration, prove control of its callback origin, prevent first-claim `appId` squatting and duplicate records, add safe credential rotation/recovery, and harden outbound URL fetching. The current registered demo is controlled; the first-registration API is not yet a public developer marketplace.
- **V4 participant cells.** Introduce a dedicated participant type script and stable campaign identity for first-class, queryable on-chain participant records. Today participant cells are recognized largely by lock and data shape, which makes discovery and settlement harder. Multi-ticket purchases and a configured ticket cap already exist; V4 is about clearer participant discovery, refund paths, and lifecycle validation without depending on mutable campaign outpoints.
- **`#Stocks` prediction markets.** Explore fully collateralized binary YES/NO markets, not actual equity stocks or leveraged short selling. A user could buy either outcome, potentially sell a position before resolution, and redeem a winning share against transparent collateral after an agreed oracle/resolution process. Order-book, AMM, and pari-mutuel constructions are still design choices; this is not a live market.
- **NDAO / DAO-yield raffle mountable.** The `NDAO.md` concept combines NervosDAO-generated yield, iCKB's more liquid access to DAO-backed value, and FON's existing round-based raffle UX. Participants would opt to pool **yield**, receive tickets according to a disclosed deposit formula, and choose to exit or stay after a round. Principal treatment, fees, yield accounting, winner tapering, and exit semantics must be explicit before implementation. This is a proposed extension, **not** current DAO integration or a claim that principal is risk-free.
- **CKB names and wallet adoption.** Let users obtain CKB names as human-readable identities for profiles, mentions, and recipients. Wallets that adopt the naming scheme could let someone send CKB to a verified name instead of manually entering an address. I have not settled the right naming or resolution approach, or received a go-ahead from people with deeper Nervos ecosystem context; I am seeking that guidance before committing to a design. Name resolution must still lead to a verified wallet destination before a transaction is signed.
- **Complete currently restricted integrations.** Finish and enable the Google Forms mountable, add clear reference-only freight `refs`, and revisit currently unavailable `@receive` streaming only with enforceable payout semantics. Expand hosted-app examples and test webhook retries, expiry, and recovery end to end.
- **Deeper review and operational hardening.** Audit contract payout and approval invariants, raffle reveal liveness and fairness, participant discovery, the off-chain/on-chain completion boundary, and deployment/monitoring. Keep push webhooks as the default; enable polling only with an appropriate scheduler and cost model.

## Links

- Repository and technical docs: https://github.com/Birdmannn/fon
- FON: https://freight43.vercel.app
- Checkbox Demo: https://checkbox-demo.vercel.app
- Mount protocol: https://github.com/Birdmannn/fon/blob/v3/MOUNT_FLOW.md

## Feedbacks

I have tightened much of the UI and contract behavior over the past months, but I wanted to release a demo now rather than wait for every edge case to be settled. I would especially appreciate feedback on the CKB contract's safety and payout rules, raffle fairness, whether the on-chain/off-chain completion split makes sense, and the security and developer experience of the mountable-app protocol. Specific failure cases, design concerns, and suggestions for what to tighten next would be very helpful.

JoyID has been my preferred wallet for testing and is the wallet used by the Checkbox Demo. I cannot yet vouch for the configuration and full transaction flow of other wallets; that integration work needs further testing and tightening. More test users, particularly for recurring raffles and mixed-wallet participation, would expose issues that my current three-wallet setup cannot reliably uncover.

**FON's interface is optimized for mobile, but I hope you can also explore it on a wider screen, ideally on your first visit. I may have left out details about the leaderboard, its perks, and other features I have forgotten to mention here. Please take some time to explore the app, and thank you for your feedback.**
